items.title: Bug: uv.lock assigns wrong source.registry to PyPI packages when a private index is configured

labels.name: needs-mre
labels.description: Needs more information for reproduction, see #9452

items.body:
### Summary

When a private index is added via [[tool.uv.index]] without explicit = true, uv sync / uv lock incorrectly records the private index URL as the source.registry for packages that were actually resolved from PyPI. The artifact download URLs (sdist, wheels) correctly point to files.pythonhosted.org, making the lockfile internally inconsistent.
This is related to #13590, but distinct: that issue involves the explicit index pattern. This issue reproduces without explicit and without [tool.uv.sources], i.e., the simpler "add a fallback private index" use case.

Example pyproject.toml
```bash
[project]
name = "uv-lock-test"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = [
    "python-dotenv",
    "my_package",
]

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "myindex"
url = "https://pyhub.myindex.de/simple"
```

Relevant environment variables set at sync time:
`UV_NATIVE_TLS=true`
`UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_USERNAME=user`
`UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_PASSWORD=password`

Notes:
- `my_package` is hosted exclusively on the private index pyhub.myindex.de
- python-dotenv is a public PyPI package not present on the private index
- No explicit = true on the index; no [tool.uv.sources] block

**Steps to Reproduce**
Start from a clean state: no uv.lock, no .venv
Set environment variables as above
Run `uv sync`

**Observed Behaviour**
python-dotenv is resolved and installed correctly. However, in the generated `uv.lock`, its source.registry is set to the private index URL, while the actual download URLs point to pythonhosted.org

```bash
[[package]]
name = "python-dotenv"
version = "1.2.2"
source = { registry = "https://pyhub.myindex.de/simple" }  # ← WRONG
sdist = { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/.../python_dotenv-1.2.2.tar.gz", ... }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/.../python_dotenv-1.2.2-py3-none-any.whl", ... },
]
```

The source.registry field points to the private index, but the actual artifact URLs are from PyPI/pythonhosted, the package was clearly fetched from PyPI, not from the private registry.

*Expected Behaviour*
python-dotenv should have source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" } in the lockfile, since it was resolved from PyPI and its artifacts are hosted there.

*Why This Matters / Potential Impact*
The lockfile is semantically incorrect and misleading
This is a silent correctness issue, the install may succeed locally, but the lockfile diverges from reality

### Platform

WSL Ubuntu 

### Version

uv 0.10.12 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

3.13.10

items.title: Support resuming interrupted package downloads

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or improvement to existing functionality

items.body:
### Summary

I’d like it if file downloads (if interrupted) could resume from the exact point where they were interrupted. A similar feature is currently in place: a cache is used for files, but there’s no solution for when a file download is interrupted—it starts over from the beginning because the streaming mode is used for downloading files. This is inconvenient for people with poor internet connections, a group to which I, unfortunately, belong. I looked for an issue with the same problem, but found only one similar one in [pip repo](https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/3128). Honestly, I'd love to see this feature, since it would make my life easier.

### Example

This feature is useful for packages like torch or tensorrt; I work with them frequently, and I find it really inconvenient that a file weighing 2.5 GiB on Windows or 900+ MB on Linux—if the download is interrupted even at 90%—doesn’t resume, but instead starts over from scratch. This takes up a lot of my time, and I think there are many people in the community who face a similar problem.

items.title: uv panics in macOS sandbox: system-configuration NULL object in SCDynamicStore
items.body:
## Summary

`uv run` panics with `Attempted to create a NULL object` when executed inside a macOS sandbox (e.g., Codex CLI sandbox). The same command succeeds outside the sandbox.

## Reproduction

```bash
# Inside macOS sandbox:
env UV_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/uv-cache uv run -- python -c "print('hi')"

# Also fails:
env UV_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/uv-cache uv python find
```

Both panic in `system-configuration` with:
```
Attempted to create a NULL object
```

The same commands succeed when run outside the sandbox.

## Environment

- **uv version:** 0.9.26
- **OS:** macOS (Darwin)
- **Context:** Running inside Codex CLI sandbox

## Root Cause (suspected)

uv appears to touch macOS reachability / `SCDynamicStore` APIs that return NULL under sandbox restrictions. The panic originates in the `system-configuration` Rust crate.

## Related

- Very similar macOS sandbox panic filed against Codex for the same crate and failure mode: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/5914

## Workaround

Setting `UV_CACHE_DIR` to a writable path resolves the cache permission issue but not the `system-configuration` panic. Falling back to direct interpreter execution (`python3 -m pytest`) works as a stopgap.

authenticate=always rejects bearer token credentials
items.body:
### Summary

`AuthMiddleware::complete_request` in `middleware.rs` (line ~554) checks:

```rust
if matches!(auth_policy, AuthPolicy::Always) && credentials.password().is_none() {
    return Err(Error::Middleware(format_err!("Missing password for {url}")));
}
```

`Credentials::Bearer` returns `None` from `password()` by design — bearer tokens are not passwords. So when a token store (like `PyxTokenStore`) returns valid bearer credentials and `authenticate = "always"` is set, this gate rejects them with "Missing password."

The check probably wants something like `credentials.is_authenticated()` or a match on the credential variant, not `password().is_none()`.

Related: #18541 (bearer auth feature request), #12313 (prior auth messaging change). This is a narrower bug in the existing gate logic.

### Platform

Linux x86_64 (code-level, platform-independent)

### Version

latest main (code read from HEAD)

items.title: Script metadata parser silently accepts duplicate script blocks

labels.name: compatibility
labels.description: Compatibility with a specification or another tool

items.body:
### Summary

`ScriptTag::parse` in `uv-scripts/src/lib.rs` finds the first `# /// script` block using `FINDER.find(contents)` (line ~500) and returns its TOML. It never checks whether the file contains a second `# /// script` block after the first one closes.

PEP 723 says tools MUST error when a script contains multiple embedded metadata blocks. Right now uv silently uses whichever one comes first and ignores any others.

A file like this should be rejected:

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = ["requests"]
# ///

print("hi")

# /// script
# dependencies = ["flask"]
# ///
```

Instead uv picks `requests` and quietly drops `flask`.

### Platform

Linux x86_64 (code-level, platform-independent)

### Version

latest main (code read from HEAD)

items.title: Panic on invalid cache-control override in index config
items.body:
### Summary

`cached_client.rs` panics when a user-configured cache-control override contains characters invalid for an HTTP header value. Two sites in `CachedClient` — `send_cached_handle_stale` (line ~575) and `fresh_request` (line ~629) — call:

```rust
http::HeaderValue::from_str(header)
    .expect("Cache-Control header must be valid UTF-8")
```

`HeaderValue::from_str` rejects more than just non-UTF-8 — any byte outside the visible ASCII range plus tab causes it to fail. A user setting something like `cache-control = "max-age=3600\x01"` in their index config will crash uv instead of getting an error message.

The value comes from `IndexCacheControl` in `index.rs`, which stores it as `Option<SmallString>` with no validation at parse time.

### Platform

Linux x86_64 (code-level, platform-independent)

### Version

latest main (code read from HEAD)

items.title: Default clone link-mode on macOS causes ~17s syspolicyd rescan on every venv recreate
items.body:
### Summary

On macOS, the default `--link-mode clone` creates new inodes for every `.so` file on each `uv pip install`. macOS syspolicyd (Gatekeeper) caches its security scan results per-inode, so every venv recreate triggers a full rescan of all native extensions — adding ~17s of wall time for a typical data science stack (pandas, polars, pyarrow, jupyterlab).

`--link-mode hardlink` avoids this because hardlinks share the uv cache's inodes, and syspolicyd recognizes them as already scanned.
## Reproduction

```bash
# Install a typical data-science stack
uv venv && VIRTUAL_ENV=.venv uv pip install pandas polars pyarrow jupyterlab

# First import — slow (~18s), expected
time .venv/bin/python -c "import pandas, polars, pyarrow"

# Second import — fast (~1s), syspolicyd cache warm
time .venv/bin/python -c "import pandas, polars, pyarrow"

# Delete and recreate with clone (default) — slow again (~18s)
rm -rf .venv
uv venv && VIRTUAL_ENV=.venv uv pip install pandas polars pyarrow jupyterlab
time .venv/bin/python -c "import pandas, polars, pyarrow"

# Delete and recreate with hardlink — FAST (~5s)
rm -rf .venv
uv venv && VIRTUAL_ENV=.venv uv pip install --link-mode hardlink pandas polars pyarrow jupyterlab
time .venv/bin/python -c "import pandas, polars, pyarrow"
```

## Root cause

1. `uv pip install` with `--link-mode clone` (default on macOS) uses `clonefile()`, which shares storage blocks but **creates a new inode** per file
2. When Python `dlopen()`s a `.so` with an inode syspolicyd hasn't seen, it performs a full security assessment (YARA scan, code signature check)
3. Unsigned `.so` files (all pip packages) trigger `errSecCSUnsigned` (-67062) and a full scan per file
4. Results are cached per-inode — but clone gives every install new inodes, defeating the cache

With `--link-mode hardlink`, the venv's `.so` files share the inode with uv's global cache. Deleting and recreating the venv reuses the same cache archive entry → same inodes → syspolicyd sees them as already scanned.

## Evidence: hardlink vs clone comparison

Tested with `uv pip install buckaroo jupyterlab polars` (108 packages, 112 `.so` files).
Monitoring `log stream --predicate 'process == "syspolicyd"'` during each import:

```
Run                                      Time     syspolicyd lines   Sample inode
A: clone, fresh install                 19.60s    3391               13301980
B: clone, delete + reinstall            18.57s    3306               13320671  (different inode)
C: hardlink, fresh install               6.14s     175               12783585
D: hardlink, delete + reinstall          5.48s     175               12783585  (same inode)
```

Clone reinstall (B) triggers a full rescan every time — new inodes, ~3300 syspolicyd log lines, ~19s.
Hardlink reinstall (D) reuses the cache's inodes — syspolicyd sees them as already scanned, ~5s.

## Per-package breakdown

Each package tested individually in a fresh clone-mode venv (cold syspolicyd),
then immediately re-imported (warm). Delta = time attributable to syspolicyd.

```
Package         Cold      Warm     Delta    .so count   .so total size
bare python    0.04s     0.03s     0.01s       10          21.1M
polars         2.43s     0.05s     2.38s        1         147.1M
pyarrow        2.47s     0.05s     2.42s       37         105.3M
pandas         9.63s     0.17s     9.46s       45          16.2M
numpy          0.46s     0.03s     0.43s       19           6.9M
jupyterlab     3.30s     0.55s     2.75s        0           0B
ALL TOGETHER  17.70s     1.02s    16.68s
```

Key observations:
- **bare python startup adds ~0s** — Python's own `.so` files live in the persistent uv-managed installation, not cloned per-venv, so they're only scanned once ever.
- **pandas is the biggest offender (9.46s / 57%)** despite only 16MB of `.so` files. It has 45 individual `.so` files, each triggering a separate syspolicyd assessment.
- **Number of `.so` files matters more than total size.** pandas (45 files, 16MB) costs 4x more than polars (1 file, 147MB).
- **jupyterlab has 0 `.so` files itself** but 2.75s delta — its deps (zmq, tornado, etc.) have native extensions.

## Relationship to existing issues

- **#9666** — attributed first-run lag to missing bytecode compilation. `--compile-bytecode` only addresses ~1s of the ~17s overhead; the remaining ~16s is syspolicyd.
- **#12904** — reporter showed `--compile-bytecode` doesn't fix the ~16s first run, consistent with syspolicyd being the dominant factor. Root cause was never identified.
- **#16726 / #16003** — Gatekeeper SIGKILL of unsigned Python interpreters. Related mechanism (syspolicyd) but different symptom (SIGKILL vs slow scan of `.so` extensions).

## Possible fixes

1. **Document the workaround.** `UV_LINK_MODE=hardlink` eliminates the rescan on reinstalls. This is a one-line config change for users.
2. **Consider changing the macOS default to `hardlink`.** The current rationale for `clone` on macOS is CoW efficiency on APFS, but hardlinks are equally storage-efficient (no data duplication) and avoid the syspolicyd penalty. The safety concern (modifying a hardlinked file corrupts the cache) only applies to the `RECORD` file, which already gets special treatment.
3. **Hybrid approach.** Use hardlink for `.so`/`.dylib` files specifically, clone for everything else.

## References

- [uv `LinkMode` default implementation](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/crates/uv-fs/src/link.rs) — macOS/iOS/Linux default to `Clone`, others to `Hardlink`
- [uv `--link-mode` docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings/#link-mode)
- [syspolicyd YARA scanning on first launch](https://lapcatsoftware.com/articles/2024/2/3.html) — documents syspolicyd scanning behavior and per-inode caching
- [APFS clonefile() creates new inodes](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/kernel/1585689-clonefile) — Apple docs confirming clones get distinct metadata (inodes)
- [#9666 — Noticeable lag with uv-created virtual environments during first interpreter session](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/9666) — attributed to missing bytecode compilation, syspolicyd not investigated
- [#12904 — Expected Impact of --compile-bytecode](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/12904) — `--compile-bytecode` doesn't explain the ~16s first-run overhead
- [#16726 — UV Python SIGKILL Issue on macOS](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16726) — Gatekeeper SIGKILL of unsigned binaries via `com.apple.provenance` xattr
- [#16003 — macOS code signing workaround](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16003) — `codesign --force -s -` workaround
- [PR #18280 — Apple Developer ID signing of release binaries](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/18280) — in-progress fix for signing uv's own binaries


Note the timings are on a Macbook Pro M4 Pro 48 GB of Ram

### Platform

Darwin 25.0.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.10.11 (006b56b12 2026-03-16)

### Python version

Python 3.13.11

## Problem

Claude Code agents can silently bypass git hooks by running git commit with the hook-skip flag. This disables pre-commit, commit-msg, and pre-push hooks — the same hooks that enforce linting, type-checking, and commit message conventions.

## Solution

Add [`block-no-verify`](https://github.com/tupe12334/block-no-verify) as a `PreToolUse` Bash hook in `.claude/settings.json`. It reads `tool_input.command` from the Claude Code hook stdin payload, detects the hook-bypass flag across all git subcommands, and exits 2 to block.

The existing `SessionStart` and `PostToolUse` hooks are preserved unchanged.

---

_Disclosure: I am the author and maintainer of `block-no-verify`._

items.title: uv lock --check --refresh false positive in workspace with [tool.uv.conflicts]
items.body:
\`uv lock --check --refresh\` reports "lockfile needs to be updated" (exit 1) even when \`uv lock --refresh\` produces a byte-for-byte identical lockfile. This is a false positive — confirmed by running \`git diff uv.lock\` immediately after, which shows zero changes.

## Minimal reproducible example

https://github.com/kingjin94/workspace-conflicts/tree/repro/uv-check-refresh-false-positive

A workspace with 4 packages each declaring conflicting prod/non-prod extras (\`psycopg2\` vs \`psycopg2-binary\`) via \`[tool.uv.conflicts]\`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kingjin94/workspace-conflicts
cd workspace-conflicts
git checkout repro/uv-check-refresh-false-positive
bash repro-check-refresh.sh
```

Full output:
```
=== Step 1: uv lock --refresh (writes result) ===
Resolved 7 packages in 170ms
Exit code: 0

=== Step 2: git diff uv.lock (should be empty) ===
No changes — lockfile is up to date

=== Step 3: uv lock --check --refresh (should also pass, but fails) ===
Resolved 7 packages in 151ms
The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--check` was provided. To update the lockfile, run `uv lock`.
Exit code: 1
```

Steps 1 and 2 prove the lockfile is genuinely current. Step 3 is a false positive.

## Notes

The workspace uses \`[tool.uv.conflicts]\` to declare prod/non-prod extras as incompatible. This generates conflict fork markers in the lockfile. The \`--check\` validation pass appears to apply different marker normalization than the write pass, causing a structural mismatch even when the lockfile content is semantically identical.

This is a distinct surviving variant after the fixes in:
- #13614 (fixed in 0.7.x — \`--check\` false positive with Python version markers)
- #15869 (fixed in 0.8.23 — \`--check\` false positive with \`include-group\` conflicts)
- #16839 (fixed in 0.10.6 — \`--dry-run\` false positive with fork markers)

Confirmed still present on 0.10.11 with a workspace using \`[tool.uv.conflicts]\` + extras.

items.body:
https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/17543 revealed that we have confusing behavior for this today.

1. If they are set but there is no content at the target, we still use the system or bundled Mozilla certificates.
2. If they are set but the content at the target is invalid, we have an empty certificate store.

For consistency with other tools, e.g., Go and OpenSSL, we should probably always have an empty certificate store if they are set to a target, regardless of whether or not the target path exists.

items.body:
### Summary

Hello!

Following the introduction of an Astral mirror which is used to fetch Ruff release metadata, Ruff, CPython and uv itself, I was wondering whether it could be made possible to customize these URLs.

In isolated environments, access to github.com or releases.astral.sh might not permitted, and it is currently impossible to proxy requests to [proxy repositories](https://help.sonatype.com/en/repository-types.html) or internal mirrors. Thus, it is impossible to download Ruff using uv, uv cannot update itself, and the uv version must be provided explicitly when installing uv using its standalone installer.

I believe that adding support for customizing the base URL of the Astral mirror could solve these issues.

I know that the updater does not fetch uv release metadata and uv archives from an Astral mirror yet, but I believe that this is already on Astral's roadmap.

Design-wise, I believe that adding configuration support using a single environment variable would be enough.

### Example

Considering that `UV_ASTRAL_MIRROR_URL` could be set to customize the base URL of the Astral mirror, it could be used as such:

```console
$ curl https://github.com/
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: github.com
$ curl https://releases.astral.sh/
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: releases.astral.sh
$ export UV_ASTRAL_MIRROR_URL="https://nexus.example.com/repository/releases.astral.sh"
$ uv python install 3.14  # uv fetches CPython from the proxy repository.
$ uv format  # uv fetches Ruff release metadata and Ruff from the proxy repository.
$ uv self update # The updater fetches uv release metadata and uv from the proxy repository.
```

### Question

items.title: Add an optional “first‑time tool execution” confirmation guard

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or improvement to existing functionality

items.body:
### Summary

`uvx` (and `uv tool run`) currently resolve, install, and execute arbitrary code with no extra friction the first time a given package is run. This makes it easy to accidentally execute unvetted code due to a typo or mistake.

I know that a typo *any* time a package name is used can run arbitrary code, like `uv add foo`. It's important to type that correctly. What's different here is that the command is run routinely and thus gets less mental focus from users. For example if you do `brew install imagemagick; magick ...` you have to be on alert for the one brew command, but typing `magic` one time you use the command instead of `magick` won't download and execute unknown code. If you're doing `uvx magick` and one time you accidentally type `uvx magic`, it will.

It would be useful to have an optional “first‑time tool execution” confirmation guard that asks for explicit consent the first time a tool is run on a machine/cache. This would be a more general fix to my [additional uvx typo traps](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/18482) proposal.

### Example

Add a configuration option, e.g., in `uv.toml`:

```toml
[tool.uv.tools]
first_run_confirmation = true
```

When `first_run_confirmation = true` and a package is about to be run via `uvx` or `uv tool run` for the first time:

  - If stderr is a TTY, prompt:

    ```text
    You are about to run `add` from PyPI for the first time.
    This will install and execute code from a third-party package.

    Proceed? [y/N]:
    ```

  - On confirmation, proceed and record that `add` has been run before; subsequent `uvx add` invocations skip the prompt.

Scope:

  - Applies when stderr is a TTY.
    - In non-interactive contexts, either don't apply the guard, or fail and add a flag to override. Former seems less intrusive.
  - Applies only to tools from registries. (Could omit trusted registries if that's a concept?)
  - Applies to `uvx <name>` and `uv tool run <name>` for consistency (though I think the latter is less of an issue).
  - `uv tool install` marks the package as previously run, that's an indication of one-time intent.
  - Not sure if some way is needed to mark a package as never run / remove from cache, maybe too niche.

items.title: uv_build fails due to uv overriding user data with normalized data
items.body: ### Summary In the public [project most important _to me_](https://pypi.org/project/hunterMakesPy/), I switched from ```toml [build-system] requires = ["setuptools", "setuptools-scm"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" ``` to ```toml [build-system] requires = ["uv_build>=0.10.0,<0.11.0"] build-backend = "uv_build" ``` I moved "./hunterMakesPy" to "./src/hunterMakesPy" even though I disagree with the "./src" convention (which is not a standard), because based on my experience with uv, I believed that if I didn't use the convention, I would have problems. I pushed the commit, and the build failed. ``` 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1144527Z Building wheels for collected packages: hunterMakesPy 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1152269Z Building wheel for hunterMakesPy (pyproject.toml): started 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1691555Z Building wheel for hunterMakesPy (pyproject.toml): finished with status 'error' 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1722777Z error: subprocess-exited-with-error 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1723595Z 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1724360Z × Building wheel for hunterMakesPy (pyproject.toml) did not run successfully. 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1725027Z │ exit code: 1 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1725422Z ╰─> [1 lines of output] 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1725952Z Error: Expected a Python module at: src/huntermakespy/__init__.py 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1726516Z [end of output] 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1726808Z 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1727314Z note: This error originates from a subprocess, and is likely not a problem with pip. 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1728007Z ERROR: Failed building wheel for hunterMakesPy 2026-03-12T15:14:27.1730036Z Failed to build hunterMakesPy ``` The problem is that when uv needs to normalize the user's data, it often permanently modifies the user's data. Compare ```cmd C:\apps\hunterMakesPy\src\hunterMakesPy>type C:\apps\hunterMakesPy\pyproject.toml [project] name = "hunterMakesPy" ``` with "uv.lock" ```toml [[package]] name = "huntermakespy" ``` The ubiquitous modification of the user's data leads to looking for a directory that doesn't exist, "src/huntermakespy," instead of the directory the user created, "src/hunterMakesPy." # Conclusion Please distinguish subroutines that - normalize data - validate data. Please confine data normalization to the subroutine that needs normalized data, and do not permanently modify the user data by replacing it with the normalized data. ### Platform ubuntu-24.04 (Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.26200.8037]) ### Version uv 0.10.9 (f675560f3 2026-03-06) ### Python version 3.14.3

items.title: How can I share a monorepo root's dev dependencies when syncing individual packages in workspace?
items.body:
### Question

Currently, it's a little tricky to verify that a given package in a monorepo does not "steal" dependencies from other packages in the workspace without testing a built wheel or discovering the issue downstream. One way that I've found is `uv sync --package package-name` and `uvx -w pytest pytest src/package-name` or `uvx -w ty ty check src/package-name`.

However, the `pytest` version is specified in the `dev` dependency-group of the root pyproject, not in `src/package-name`. My following question is possibly related to [issue #8949](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/8949). Since this is tooling-specific and not related to published dependencies, is there a way (or could there be a way) to only specify a `pytest` (or other developer tool) version in the project root, to be shared when doing something like `uv sync --package package-name`? Presumably the interface would be slightly different. 

I've also tried something like `uvx -w pytest==version pytest src/package-name/`, but that requires consistently updating the command (if it exists in some CI workflow file or shell history) to match the version specified in the root pyproject. Furthermore, it is unable to access packages in the virtual environment, leading to import errors.

I would prefer to keep the ergonomics of a workspace, but I'm open to options. What is the intended workflow here? Preferably, it would not involve manually maintaining consistent versions of developer dependencies in all packages in the monorepo.

items.title: constraint-dependencies ignored for transitive dep, leading to multiple versions of package in uv.lock
items.body:
### Summary

MRE: https://github.com/tsudol-plaid/uv-brotlicffi-doubled

We're migrating a monorepo from requirements.txt/`pip compile` to `uv`.  We have a monorepo-wide one-version policy, which is currently enforced by `pip compile` putting every project's requirements into a single `requirements.txt` for the whole monorepo. We're moving to a `uv` workspace with a single `uv.lock`.

We currently have both `requirements.txt` and `uv.lock` while we're migrating. The lockfile is generated by updating `requirements.txt`, then using the contents of that file to set `tools.uv.constraint-dependencies` and `project.dependencies` in the workspace `pyproject.toml`. We then run `uv lock --upgrade` to update the lock file with all the package changes.   
We also run a linter to check that `uv.lock` and `requirements.txt` are up-to-date by regenerating them and checking that nothing changed. This works well as long as all dependencies are pinned, and we make sure they are.

Today that linter due to `uv lock` updating a package, `brotlicffi`: `Updated brotlicffi v1.1.0.0, v1.2.0.0 -> v1.1.0.0, v1.2.0.1`. We pin `brotlicffi==1.1.0.0` in `requirements.txt`, so it's very surprising to see _two_ versions of this package in `uv.lock`! (v1.2.0.1 was just published earlier today, hence the change.) 

The `brotlicffi` dependency comes from `ddgs`, which depends on `httpx[brotli]`, which has an [unpinned dependency](https://github.com/encode/httpx/blob/0.28.1/pyproject.toml#L39-L42) on `brolticffi`.

So there are 2 surprising behaviors here:
- `brotlicffi` is pinned to `1.1.0.0` in `constraint-dependencies` but `uv` ignores it, leading to `1.2.0.1` being brought in.
- `uv` allows 2 versions of the same package in `uv.lock`.

I suspect that `brotlicffi` having a marker is also a factor here.

I was able to resolve the double versioning by removing the `brotlicffi` entry from `requirements.txt` (and therefore the project's dependencies and constraint-dependencies), then regenerating the file (creating a pin on `brotlicffi==1.2.0.1` instead) and re-running `uv.lock`. However, I'm worried that future releases of `brotlicffi` could cause the same problem.

It's reasonable to say that this is a weird edge case brought on by our mid-migration setup, and we'll stop being at risk of this once we're fully on `uv`. (Or to put it another way: we're playing silly games and winning silly prizes.)

### Platform

Darwin 24.6.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.10.4 (Homebrew 2026-02-17)

### Python version

Python 3.10.16

items.title: local editable dependencies: `uv lock` behaves differently for projects and scripts
items.body:
### Summary

When a script references a local editable dependency and that dependency's `pyproject.toml` changes (e.g., a transitive dependency version is updated), `uv lock --script` does **not** update the script lockfile. The lockfile silently remains stale. Running `uv run --locked --script` then uses the outdated locked versions.

The equivalent project command (`uv lock`) correctly detects the same change and updates the lockfile as expected. The inconsistency is limited to `uv lock --script`.

### Minimal reproduction

The full repository is available at: <https://github.com/Weidav/uv-lock-bug-minimal-example>

### Steps to reproduce

Clone the repo and execute `./reproduce_bug.sh`.
The script also explains in detail the expected vs actual behavior at each step.

To clean up afterwards, run `./reset.sh`, then the workspace will be back to the initial state.

### Expected behavior

`uv lock --script <script>` should re-read the `pyproject.toml` of local editable dependencies (just as `uv lock` does for projects) and update the script lockfile when those dependencies have changed.

After updating pydantic, `uv run --locked --script example-script.py` should fail and after running `uv lock --script example-script.py`, `example-script.py.lock` should contain `pydantic==2.12.5`.

I would expect the same behavior from scripts and project. I think the projects behave correctly and as documented, but the scripts do not.

### Actual behavior

`uv lock --script <script>` does not detect that a local editable dependency's `pyproject.toml` has changed. The script lockfile remains unchanged (still pinning `pydantic==1.10.26`) and `uv run --locked --script` does not raise a lockfile mismatch error — it silently runs with the stale dependencies.

### Workaround

Explicitly pass `--upgrade-package` for the local editable dependency:

```bash
uv lock --script example-script.py --upgrade-package example-lib
```

This forces uv to re-resolve the dependency and picks up the new transitive constraints, but this should not be necessary after a normal `uv lock --script`.

### Additional notes

- The bug does **not** affect `uv lock` (project mode) — only `uv lock --script` (inline script mode).
- Clearing the uv cache (`uv cache clean`) does not resolve the issue, confirming this is not a caching problem.
- The bug means scripts using local editable path sources can silently run with stale transitive dependencies, even when `--locked` is specified. This undermines the reproducibility guarantee that `--locked` is supposed to provide.


### Platform

Linux 6.8.0-1044-azure x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Version

uv 0.10.8

### Python version

Python 3.12.1

items.title: `uv pip install` resolved packages difference compared to `pip install`
items.body:
### Summary

We are recently switch to uv from python native pip (as pip occasionally fails resolving complicate dependencies and is very slow). Thanks for your hard work! 
However, we oberserved difference behaviors in one case:

We have below dependency:
```
`myproject_c` -------> `h5py >= 3.14.0`
              |------> `myproject_b`  ------> `myproject_c` ----> `h5py == 3.15.0`
```

We expected `myproject_b`, `myproject_c` to be installed when doing `uv pip install myproject_c` and the `h5py` finally be resolved to `3.15.0` (`myproject_c` need ping to a fixed version of `h5py` for some reason)

However, what actually happens it that, it first install `h5py 3.15.1` (the latest version), and then find that is a conflict due to `myproject_c` requires `h5py == 3.15.0`, then it tries to lower down the version of `myproject_c` until it finds a very old version of  `myproject_c` that doesn't ping on `h5py` version. 

Interesting, if I change the order of dependency to below:
```
`myproject_c` -------> `myproject_b`  ------> `myproject_c` ----> `h5py == 3.15.0`
              |------> `h5py >= 3.14.0`
```

Then it can correctly resolve `h5py` to `3.15.0` with the latest version of `myproject_c`. 

I also verify this case with python native pip and it can correctly resolve `h5py` to `3.15.0` no matter which order it is. 

I guess uv internally do some DFS-like algorithm to resolve the dependency? I cannot say it is absolute wrong, but at least I feel python native pip's behavior make more sense to me.

Below is the verbose output from `uv pip install myproject_c`:

[stdout.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25725867/stdout.txt)

### Platform

macOS 26 arm64

### Version

uv 0.10.7 (Homebrew 2026-02-27)

items.body:
### Summary

GitHub recently added a platform feature which allows marking releases as immutable: https://github.blog/changelog/2025-10-28-immutable-releases-are-now-generally-available/

This new configuration option provides the following benefits (see [docs](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/immutable-releases)): 
> * Git tags cannot be moved or deleted: Once an immutable release is published, its associated Git tag is locked to a specific commit and cannot be changed or removed.
> * Release assets cannot be modified or deleted: All files attached to the release (such as binaries and archives) are protected from modification or deletion.

The new setting requires explicit opt-in (at the org or repo level), and only affects new releases published after it has been enabled (see [instructions](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/secure-your-supply-chain/establish-provenance-and-integrity/preventing-changes-to-your-releases)).

It would be nice to enable it for future `uv` releases, in order to ensure that a given released version will always corresponds to a stable set of `[git-tag, artifacts, attestation]`.

items.title: Divergence from pip-compile when using `--upgrade` and `--upgrade-package`
items.body:
### Summary

Hi folks! Been slowly migrating to use uv's pip-compile compatibility and stumbled across a divergence in behavior when passing both `--upgrade` (upgrade all packages) and `--upgrade-package={pkg}{constraint}` (upgrade package {pkg}, subject to {constraint}).

jazzband's pip-compile currently does it's best to respect the intention of both flags -- it considers the additional constraint and maximizes packages upgrades while still satisfying the constraint. It appears that `uv` simply ignores any additional constraints when alongside `--upgrade`.

<details>
<summary> A minimal repro: </summary>

```dockerfile
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.10.0-debian-slim

WORKDIR /mre

RUN uv venv --quiet && uv pip install --quiet 'pip-tools==7.5.2' 'pip<26'
RUN echo "requests" > requirements.in && \
  echo "requests==2.28.0" > requirements-pipcompile.txt && \
  echo "requests==2.28.0" > requirements-uv.txt

# pip-compile
RUN .venv/bin/pip-compile --quiet requirements.in -o requirements-pipcompile.txt \
    --upgrade --upgrade-package 'requests<2.30.0' && \
  echo "requests version with pip-compile:" && \
  grep "^requests==" requirements-pipcompile.txt

# uv
RUN uv pip compile --quiet requirements.in -o requirements-uv.txt \
    --upgrade --upgrade-package 'requests<2.30.0' && \
  echo "requests version with uv pip compile:" && \
  grep "^requests==" requirements-uv.txt
```
</details>

```console
$ docker build -f ./Dockerfile . --progress=plain --no-cache
...

#8 6.363 requests version with pip-compile:
#8 6.364 requests==2.29.0

...
#9 1.755 requests version with uv pip compile:
#9 1.756 requests==2.32.5
```

I was curious, so I peeked through the code and found [this TODO](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/474eb056347c0160bc2db416e612ecc8096722e6/crates/uv-configuration/src/package_options.rs#L154-L155) that seems pertinent.

From my understanding, we _DO_ want uv's pip-compile to be a drop in replacement, so I think it fair to consider this a bug worth fixing! I've been working on a patch that should handle this case (as well as a few related situations with `--no-upgrade` etc).. I'll link to that from here, if that's ok!

### Platform

Ubuntu 24.04 (x84_64), though think this is OS, architecture independent

### Version

uv 0.10.7

### Python version

Python 3.14.0

items.title: Include earliest valid date in `exclude-newer` resolver hint
items.body:
Follow-up from https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/18217#discussion_r2865246666

When `--exclude-newer` filters out all versions of a package, the resolver now emits a hint (added in #18217):

```
hint: `iniconfig` was filtered by `exclude-newer` to only include packages uploaded before 2000-0101T00:00:00Z. Consider using `exclude-newer-package` to override the cutoff for this package.
```

It would be useful to also include the earliest date that would allow at least one version of the package to be resolved. Since we have access to the index at hint-generation time, we can look up the upload timestamps and find the minimum value that would unblock resolution.

For example:

```
hint: `iniconfig` was filtered by `exclude-newer` to only include packages uploaded before 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z. The earliest available version was published on 2020-10-19T00:00:00Z. Consider using `exclude-newer-package` to override the cutoff for this package.
```

items.title: Proposal: Official `.uv` file extension for portable PEP 723 scripts where `uv` is the sole dependency
items.body:
## Summary

Recognize `.uv` as the conventional extension for single-file Python scripts combining a `uv run --script` shebang with [PEP 723](https://peps.python.org/pep-0723/) inline metadata. This gives a clear, at-a-glance signal that a script is **fully portable** — requiring only `uv` to run.

## Motivation

```python
#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10,<=3.13"
# dependencies = ["requests", "rich"]
# ///

import requests
from rich import print
print(requests.get("https://httpbin.org/get").json())
```

This script can be `chmod +x`'d and run on any machine with uv installed. No virtualenv, no pip, no setup. That's a fundamentally different contract than a `.py` file — but today there's no way to tell them apart without opening the file.

## The Proposed `.uv` Contract

While anything could be considered a `.uv` script, the priorities are stability, simplicity, and confidence.

In order to meet these values, I would suggest we either require (or strongly suggest) that `.uv` scripts adhere to the following:

1. Use "max" version constraints on all dependencies, including and especially on the Python version itself. Prevents breakage in future when new releases inevitably add new volatility into the dependency trees.
2. Include the shebang string so they can be called without passing an interpreter.


## Prior art

Python already uses extensions to signal alternate launchers/runtimes:

- `.pyw` — run with `pythonw` (no console)
- [`.pyz`](https://peps.python.org/pep-0441/) — ZIP application (PEP 441, bundled runnable)
- [`.pex`](https://docs.pex-tool.org/whatispex.html) — self-contained executable venv
- `.ipy` — IPython script
- [`.xsh`](https://xon.sh/) — Xonsh shell script
- [`.sage`](https://www.sagemath.org/) — SageMath script
- [`.pyx`](https://cython.readthedocs.io/) — Cython source

`.uv` fits the **"alternate launcher"** category alongside `.pyw` — "run me with `uv`."

## Concrete asks

1. **Docs**: Mention `.uv` as a recommended extension in the [Running scripts](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/scripts/) guide.
2. **`uv init --script`**: Consider generating `my_tool.uv` (or offering it) with shebang + PEP 723 block pre-populated.
3. **Editor support**: Recommend a VS Code `files.associations` snippet; file a [github/linguist](https://github.com/github/linguist) PR for GitHub syntax highlighting.
4. **Linters**: Document [ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) config like `extend-include = ["*.uv"]`.

## Benefits

- **Visual signal**: `ls` immediately distinguishes portable uv scripts from regular `.py` files.
- **CI-friendly**: `**/*.uv` globs can enforce valid PEP 723 metadata + shebangs.
- **Encodes a contract**: A `.py` file *might* have inline metadata. A `.uv` file *always* does.
- **Zero execution impact**: The OS uses the shebang; `uv run` reads file contents. The extension is purely a human/tooling convention.

## Alternatives considered

- **`.uv.py`** — All `.py` tooling works, but clunky; double extensions uncommon in Python.
- **`.uv-py`** — Loses `.py` tooling support *and* is less clean than `.uv`.
- **Status quo** — Portable scripts stay invisible; no way to enforce the contract via file patterns.

## Concerns

- **Extension collision**: `.uv` exists in 3D modeling (UV texture coords). Zero practical overlap with Python.
- **Editor support**: Most editors detect Python from the shebang. A one-line config handles the rest.
- **Adoption**: Fully opt-in. Existing `.py` + PEP 723 scripts keep working.

```py
x = None
```

```py
x = None
while True:
    x

    reveal_type(x)  # None
```
